title: Praise is not proof
principle: Praise is not proof. Money or a firm promise is.

screens.text: Let me tell you about a scooter. In July 2021, Ola Electric let people book its new electric scooter online. You paid ₹499, and you could get it back if you changed your mind. Ola said it got 1 lakh bookings in the first 24 hours.

screens.prompt: Do you think 1 lakh bookings at ₹499 proved that 1 lakh people would buy the scooter?

options.label: Yes. They all paid real money
Partly. It was a small, safe yes

screens.why: Partly. A ₹499 booking you can get back shows real interest, but it costs almost nothing. The true test comes when people must pay much more.

screens.title: Asking for more
screens.text: In September, the real sale opened. Buyers now paid a ₹20,000 advance, which they could get back until the scooter left the factory. Each step asked for more. Ola announced big sales in rupees but never said how many scooters were ordered, so nobody knows how many bookers paid more.

screens.title: Commitment
screens.text: Rob Fitzpatrick, who wrote The Mom Test, a book about customers, says: look at what people give up for you. A compliment costs nothing, so it proves nothing. Real proof is commitment: their time, their name, or their money. The more they give up, the stronger it is.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: Ola is a big company, but the same idea works for your home bakery. Ten friends see your cake photos and say, "Great idea! You should start!" Your first Diwali as a home baker is coming, and you're planning your first big week.

screens.prompt: Ten friends said "Great idea!" about your cakes. How many Diwali orders do you have so far?

options.label: About five, since half usually buy

screens.why: Right. Praise costs your friends nothing, so it isn't an order. You'll still bake for Diwali, but count only the people who commit.

wrong.b: That turns every compliment into a sale. Praise costs nothing, so it doesn't promise a single cake.
wrong.c: "About half" is a guess with nothing behind it. No friend has ordered or paid, so you have none yet.

screens.prompt: A school principal says, "Lovely cakes! Bring samples on Monday, and I'll introduce you to our canteen head." What has she given you?

options.label: Just praise, since she hasn't paid
A firm order for the canteen

screens.why: Yes. These aren't kind words about your idea: she's promising a meeting and an introduction. That costs her time and her good name, so it means more than praise.

wrong.a: No money yet, true. But a meeting and an introduction cost her time and her good name. Praise costs nothing; this doesn't.
wrong.b: Not an order yet: the canteen head hasn't agreed to anything. But the meeting and the introduction are real steps towards one.

screens.prompt: Mothers pay ₹200 advances on ₹700 Diwali cakes that cost you ₹350. If one never collects and nobody else buys it, what do you lose?
screens.why: Right. You spent ₹350 and keep her ₹200, so you lose ₹150. An advance of ₹350 would cover your cost in full. Set your advance to at least what the cake costs you.

wrong.a: Her ₹200 helps, but the cake cost you ₹350. ₹350 − ₹200 = ₹150 lost. A ₹350 advance would cover it.
wrong.c: You do keep her ₹200 advance. So the loss is ₹350 − ₹200 = ₹150.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six things people did after seeing your cakes. For each one, tell me: did they give up something real?

items.text: Paid a ₹200 advance for a Diwali cake
Introduced you to her society secretary
Spent Sunday morning helping you take orders at the society gate

screens.why: Money, a Sunday morning, and an introduction that uses her good name all cost something. Compliments, likes and "I'll tell everyone" cost nothing.

screens.setup: Diwali is three weeks away. 25 friends and neighbours have praised your cakes, but not ordered. 8 other mothers have paid a ₹350 advance. Each cake sells for ₹700 and costs you ₹350 to make. You can bake at most 30 that week, and you buy ingredients a week ahead.
screens.question: How do you plan your Diwali baking?

options.label: Bake 30, to be ready for the 25 and for walk-ins
options.outcome: All 8 paid orders are collected, and 6 more people buy at the door. 16 cakes are left over. That's ₹5,600 of ingredients and gas wasted.
options.why: You planned around praise. Only the 8 advances were real, and praise doesn't turn into buyers by itself.
options.better: Message the 25 first: orders need a ₹350 advance by Sunday.

options.label: Bake 12: the 8 paid orders plus 4 spare
options.outcome: All 8 orders are collected, 3 spares sell at the door, and 1 is left. Later, two friends who praised you ask why you never told them to order.
options.why: Planning around paid orders kept you safe. But you never asked the 25 to commit, so you may have missed real buyers.
options.better: Message the 25 first: orders need a ₹350 advance by Sunday.

options.label: Message the 25: orders need ₹350 by Sunday
options.outcome: Six more pay by Sunday, so you have 14 paid orders. You bake 16. All 14 are collected, and the 2 spares sell at the door.
options.why: You turned praise into a real yes or no before you bought anything. Asking for an advance is a kind way to learn the truth.

screens.text: A compliment costs ___, so it proves nothing. A ₹350 advance from a buyer is ___.
screens.why: Exactly. Ola asked for ₹499, then ₹20,000. Your mothers paid ₹350, and the principal gave you her time. What people give up is the proof.

summary: Commitment: what people give up for you: their time, their name or their money.
A compliment costs nothing, so it proves nothing.
Ask for an advance that covers your cost. It turns praise into a real yes or no.

cards.front: Which is real proof that someone wants your product?
cards.back: Money given up is proof. Praise costs nothing.

cards.front: 12 people pay a ₹100 advance on ₹400 orders. How much is still to come?
A shop owner introduces you to his supplier. What did he give up?
cards.back: He put his name behind you. That's a real commitment.
